readerTitle: The tomatoes, the chef and the phone number
caseNote: 가상 사례 (농장-식당 직거래 마켓플레이스, 프리랜서 경리 매칭 플랫폼) · 실제 기업이나 수치는 쓰지 않음
insight: 마켓플레이스를 시작할 때는 넓게 펼치기보다 좁고 촘촘하게 시작해 거래가 실제로 성사되게 하고, 그다음에는 연결 이후에도 계속 머물 이유를 만들어야 한다.
misconception: 공급자와 구매자를 많이 모아 연결만 해 주면 마켓플레이스가 굴러가고, 직거래는 규칙으로 막으면 된다.

sources.text: BMO-05 유닛의 개념 레슨 (유동성, 탈중개화)에서 다룬 표준 마켓플레이스 개념
모든 인물, 사업, 상황은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 사례는 가상이며 통계나 실제 기업 사실을 쓰지 않았습니다. 식당이 납품 대금을 일정 기간 후 지급하는 관행은 일반적 설명으로만 썼고 특정 일수는 '보통'이라는 표현 없이 예시 조건(30일)으로만 제시했습니다. 게시 전 표현이 단정적으로 읽히지 않는지 확인하세요.
7번 카드의 '배송 트럭, 결제 선지급 비용이 수수료로 감당되어야 한다'는 일반 원리입니다. 구체적 수수료율은 적지 않았습니다. BMO-05-03(수수료율), BMO-05-10과 겹치지 않는지 확인하세요.
BMO-05-07(과외 마켓플레이스) 적용 레슨과 판단 문제가 겹치지 않는지 확인하세요. 이 레슨은 유동성(좁은 지역 출시)과 탈중개화(반복 B2B 거래)에 집중합니다.

cards.title: The tomatoes, the chef and the phone number
body: Maya used to cook in a busy restaurant. Every summer she watched two things happen at once. Small farms nearby threw away crates of tomatoes they couldn't sell. Her chef wanted local produce but had no time to call twelve farms every week.
So Maya decides to build a marketplace that connects them. Farms list what they've harvested. Restaurants order. She takes a cut. Simple, on paper.

image.label: Crates of tomatoes at a farm on one side, a busy restaurant kitchen on the other
image.brief: 화면 왼쪽에 작은 농장의 토마토 상자들(일부는 시들기 시작), 오른쪽에 바쁜 식당 주방에서 메뉴를 고민하는 셰프. 가운데에 빈 연결선이 그려져 있음. 따뜻한 일러스트 톤, 실제 브랜드나 로고 없음.

cards.title: Where should Maya launch?
body: Maya has enough money for one delivery van and six months of work. Farms and restaurants across the whole region say they're interested.

options.text: Sign up as many farms and restaurants as possible across the region
options.feedback: The listings look impressive, but they're spread thin. A chef rarely finds what she needs nearby, and farms rarely get orders. That's weak **liquidity**: lots of members, few deals.

options.text: Start with 8 farms and 25 restaurants on one delivery route, and a short list of core items
options.feedback: Small and dense means most searches end in an order and most harvests sell. You give up reach for now to get **liquidity**, the thing that makes both sides come back.

options.text: Sign up lots of farms first, then find restaurants later
options.feedback: Picking a side to build first is sensible. But produce spoils in days. Farms with no buyers this week won't list again next week.

cards.title: Small and busy beat big and empty.
body: Maya chose one route. In the first weeks, chefs who logged in usually found tomatoes, greens and eggs for Thursday delivery. Farmers saw most of their listings sell.
This is **liquidity**: the chance that a buyer finds what they want, and a seller finds a buyer, quickly. A marketplace with 25 busy restaurants can feel more alive than one with 200 quiet ones.
Fresh food makes the test harsher. A unsold sofa can wait a month. An unsold lettuce cannot.

cards.title: Each side asks one question.
body: Maya tracks one simple answer for each side every week, not the total number of sign-ups.

breakdown.label: The chef's question
breakdown.detail: Can I get what I need for this week's menu?

breakdown.label: The farmer's question
breakdown.detail: Will this harvest sell in the next few days?

breakdown.label: Liquidity
breakdown.detail: When both answers are usually yes, both sides come back

cards.softwareNote: In a software marketplace, the same check is a search-to-transaction rate: how often a search or listing ends in a deal. It tells you more than total users.

cards.title: Chef Luis asks for the farmer's number.
body: Three months in, Luis orders eggs from farmer Ana every single week. He likes them so much he asks Ana for her phone number. Why pay Maya's cut when they could just text each other?
This is **disintermediation**: buyer and seller meet through a marketplace, then deal directly and cut it out.
The risk is highest exactly where Maya's business looks healthiest: the same two businesses, trading the same goods, every week.

image.label: A chef and a farmer swapping phone numbers next to a delivery crate
image.brief: 식당 뒷문에서 셰프와 농부가 달걀 상자 옆에 서서 휴대폰을 맞대고 번호를 교환하는 장면. 뒤쪽에 마켓플레이스 배송 밴이 조금 멀어지는 모습. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: How should Maya respond?
body: More pairs like Luis and Ana are forming. Maya needs them to keep ordering through her. What's her best move?

options.text: Ban sharing contact details and suspend anyone caught trading directly
options.feedback: Rules are easy to break with one quiet text. Policing also sours the relationships her marketplace depends on, and it fights **disintermediation** without giving anyone a reason to stay.

options.text: Make staying worth it: one delivery from many farms, one weekly invoice, farms paid fast while restaurants pay later
options.feedback: Ana can't deliver greens from four other farms, and Luis can't get 30 days to pay from her. When the marketplace does work neither side wants to do, **disintermediation** stops making sense.

options.text: Cut the fee to almost zero for repeat pairs
options.feedback: A tiny fee removes the reason to leave, but it also removes Maya's income from her best customers. It can work as one piece, not as the whole answer.

cards.title: The value you add has a cost.
body: A shared delivery van, fast payments to farms and weekly invoices all cost real money. Paying farms before restaurants pay her means Maya carries that cash gap herself.
Her cut has to cover these costs, or the features that keep people from leaving will sink the business.
And some pairs will leave anyway. That can be fine if they are few. The goal is to keep most of the trade, not every single egg.

cards.title: Now it's a bookkeeping marketplace.
body: You run an online platform that matches small businesses with freelance bookkeepers. Once a match works, the client and bookkeeper often start paying each other directly. Which move best protects your business?

options.text: Build tools both sides use every month: a shared document portal, automatic invoicing, payment protection
options.feedback: Like Maya's single delivery and invoice, daily-use tools make the platform part of the work. **Disintermediation** loses its appeal when leaving means giving up something useful.

options.text: Charge one finder's fee on the first month, then step aside
options.feedback: You accept **disintermediation** and price for it up front. It's honest and simple, but you earn once from relationships that may last years.

options.text: Hide bookkeepers' names and photos until a client hires one
options.feedback: Clients choosing someone to handle their finances want to know who they are. Hiding names hurts trust and the match rate, and the details still leak after hiring.

cards.title: Start dense, then earn every repeat order.
body: Two ideas did the work here. **Liquidity:** Maya launched on one route so most orders and harvests found a match. **Disintermediation:** once pairs formed, she kept them by doing work neither side wanted to do alone.
**Try it today:** pick your best repeat customer or supplier. Write down one thing you do for them that they couldn't easily get by going direct.
